channel.title: Ayiti Sitwayen · Candidates under scrutiny
channel.description: Understand the record, follow the money and examine documented connections. Each article follows one question in plain language.

item.title: Martine Moïse and malaria: what became of the 2020 goal?
item.description: In 2018, she backed malaria elimination. Health data for 2025 show the disease persisted. They raise a policy-continuity question without assigning one person all national outcomes.

item.title: Martine Moïse and Dermalog: a signature and influence are different questions
item.description: An identity-card contract, influence allegations and an explicit denial: following the decisions means keeping a complaint distinct from a conviction.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu vs Jude Célestin: after the financing, what assets and services remain?
item.description: A private hotel and public equipment are different records. Both show why financing figures need accounts of what they delivered.

item.title: Jean Ernest Muscadin vs Munir Mourra: an armored vehicle is not a security budget
item.description: Citizens can buy equipment. A state must fund its use, maintenance and oversight for years. Those responsibilities deserve examining together.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Joanas Gué: buying local means paying producers on time
item.description: Using food purchases to support local production was on the table in 2010. This comparison follows the path from contract to delivery and payment.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs René St-Fort: who makes sure the teacher gets paid?
item.description: A common curriculum and a larger budget can help schools. Money must also reach the teacher, on the date it is due.

item.title: Dominique Dupuy vs Savannah Savary: the same precision, different rules for money
item.description: A diplomatic-spending decision and an account of family businesses are different records. They help identify what the public needs to assess each candidate.

item.title: Clarens Renois vs Junior Salomon: what oversight remains when allies hold power?
item.description: A signature on the 2024 pact and an OPL protest in 2025 show why political accountability needs more than ally or opponent labels.

item.title: Olivier Barrau vs Munir Mourra: an agricultural bank needs an answer when a harvest fails
item.description: Credit, irrigation and insurance belong to the same farming season. They address different problems, but their rules need to work together.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu vs Jacky Lumarque: a scholarship must identify who pays and who selects
item.description: Both attended a 2020 scholarship launch. That connection does not merge the programmes into one fund or make the financing a personal gift.

item.title: Claude Joseph vs Etzer Emile: emergency powers and capacity that must endure
item.description: One headed a cabinet after the president’s assassination. The other proposes expanding police. The comparison follows deadlines, oversight and what lasts after the first announcement.

item.title: Jean Ernest Muscadin vs Michel Martelly: public protection needs answers about power
item.description: A UN report about a prosecutor and U.S. sanctions against a former president are different records. They require distinct evidentiary paths and the same precision.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Jerry Tardieu: who chooses the road, and who maintains it?
item.description: A large investment plan and a debate over departmental power meet at one question: how does a national decision keep serving a commune?

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Olivier Barrau: after a loss, who carries the cost?
item.description: A loan can start or expand an activity. Insurance can help after a shock. Comparing these records means following risk as well as announced money.

item.title: Michel Martelly vs Etzer Emile: follow school money into the classroom
item.description: A transfer-fee record and two budget targets show why money collected, authorized and spent must remain distinct.

item.title: Martine Moïse vs Claude Joseph: one killing, different judicial roles
item.description: A survivor and a former prime minister appear at different judicial stages. Election registration neither erases those records nor supplies a verdict on them.

item.title: Walsonn Sanon vs Clarens Renois: rejecting one pact, signing another
item.description: The agreements and years differ. Their positions allow scrutiny of participation in transitional decisions and how leaders account for those choices.

item.title: Jude Elie vs Wilner Joseph: an institution’s name does not explain a person’s role
item.description: A NYCHA chart and a report identifying a government adviser provide two starting points. Roles, dates and outcomes need separating before experience can be assessed.

item.title: Gandhy Dorfeuille vs Joanas Gué: after the launch, does the service last?
item.description: Electricity and irrigation are different services. Both require tracing money through completed work to the maintenance people need afterward.

item.title: Déus Deronneth vs Marc-Arthur Drouillard: a result is not the whole election story
item.description: One obtained a changed result after challenges. The other announced withdrawal to support Jovenel Moïse. These are different political acts to examine.

item.title: Kely Bastien vs Junior Salomon: a Senate title does not explain all the power
item.description: Their records raise different questions: how a leader accounts for his decisions, and how he obtains authority to lead.

item.title: Daniest Adrien vs Ricardo Jean Pierre: a party slate is not its vote total
item.description: PRC has more Senate entries; PANAH has one more deputy entry. The data show participation in the contest without predicting who will win.

item.title: Martine Moïse joins the list: 33 presidential registrations
item.description: Three women appear in the late November 15 reading. Registration opens a record to examine; it is neither final approval nor a measure of election chances.

item.title: Savannah Savary vs Olivier Barrau: family businesses and the public interest
item.description: Their business histories explain part of their careers. The public question concerns what they control today and the safeguards they accept for tomorrow.

item.title: Wilson Jeudy vs Jude Célestin: public works must account for the people affected
item.description: Delmas camp clearances and CNE equipment purchases are different records. They offer two ways to examine authority, resources and public service.

item.title: Hans Joseph vs Lucmanne Delille: an investigation must reach a judge
item.description: A former ULCC head and a former justice minister held different responsibilities. Their records direct attention to the full justice process, beyond an investigation’s announcement.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque vs René St-Fort: from the lesson to a student’s life
item.description: Training experience and proposals on teachers’ conditions address different parts of the same chain. Access, learning and what follows all need examination.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Munir Mourra: doubling police is not doubling budgets
item.description: Two security proposals use doubling. One counts people; the other counts money. The outcome for citizens requires more than those figures.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Moïse Durocher: what counts as a job?
item.description: A small-business loan, temporary employment and a lasting job are different outcomes. Campaign totals need common definitions before comparison.

item.title: Clarens Renois vs Maxo Joseph: a church agreement does not own anyone’s vote
item.description: They participated in the same political process in 2015. Later records show why alliances need dates and support networks must be distinguished from voters’ rights.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu vs Gary Bodeau: who controlled access in Parliament?
item.description: The 2019 record raises access to documents. U.S. sanctions against Bodeau raise a separate question about money and influence that must remain distinct.

item.title: Dominique Dupuy vs Claude Joseph: after diplomatic words, what protection?
item.description: The former foreign ministers bring different records at the same border. A public stance alone does not measure what changed for citizens.

item.title: Michel Martelly vs Jocelerme Privert: two presidents, different accountability tests
item.description: Martelly’s school promise and Privert’s transitional mandate are different records. Comparing them requires separating money, authority and deadlines.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu vs Olivier Barrau: business experience must show whom it serves
item.description: A hotel and an insurer received international financing. Comparing the records means following the money to the people it was intended to help.

item.title: Etzer Emile vs Jean Ernest Muscadin: more police, accountable to whom?
item.description: One offers police recruitment targets. The other has a prosecutorial record that raises questions about the use of force. Security requires examining both.

item.title: After parties choose, public debate should begin
item.description: Our view: nomination should open a programme to public scrutiny rather than close questions inside an organization.

item.title: An institution-funded scholarship should remain a civic opportunity
item.description: Our view: crediting someone who opens a door should never create a political obligation for the recipient.

item.title: Security should give citizens protection they can trust
item.description: Our view: anger at gang violence requires a state response that protects life and answers for its own use of force.

item.title: When examining a candidate’s family, follow the exercise of power
item.description: Our view: inheritance, appointments and business interests merit precise scrutiny. Kinship does not establish guilt.

item.title: A transition needs an exit beyond its leader’s discretion
item.description: Our view: security conditions need public measures, and temporary mandates need enforceable limits.

item.title: Public money, private money: candidates should make the distinction visible
item.description: Our view: a popular name or compelling story should not replace financial records that allow citizens to scrutinize power.

item.title: Before Martine Moïse’s entry: Dupuy and Savary in the 32-name list
item.description: The earlier November 15 reading had two entries coded F among 32. Martine Moïse’s later entry brought the list to 33, with three coded F. These are two points in a changing registry.

item.title: Lucmanne Delille: a signature on police officers’ right to organize
item.description: The March 2020 order supplies a concrete measure in his ministerial record. Signing a text and securing its implementation are connected tasks.

item.title: The decree Hans Joseph criticized: which gate must a case pass?
item.description: The December 2025 text places a parliamentary step in the prosecution of certain senior officials. Its own preamble acknowledges an inoperative legislature.

item.title: Martelly’s asset disclosures: why 20 plus 17 does not automatically mean 37
item.description: ULCC’s allegations require precise scrutiny. Accounts counted at different times are not necessarily different accounts.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu and French scholarships: who financed the opportunity?
item.description: A deputy’s role in assembling partners deserves recognition. Institutional funding and work also need to remain visible.

item.title: Wilner Joseph: from advising government to competing for office
item.description: Government relationships need documentation. They establish neither control of government nor a reason to ignore electoral fairness.

item.title: Claude Joseph, EDE and Smith Augustin: what responsibility does a party carry?
item.description: A party defended its representative, then sought his resignation. The sequence invites scrutiny of political decisions without transferring criminal allegations between people.

item.title: Martelly in the Moïse inquiry in July 2026: testimony is not conviction
item.description: A judicial appearance is a specific event. It should be kept distinct from other allegations or sanctions concerning the former president.

item.title: Claude Joseph: what the 2022 Dominican entry ban establishes
item.description: His name appeared in an instruction containing other names. That alone does not establish a criminal relationship among them.

item.title: Michelet Nestor in 2015: defending people of Haitian descent beyond a slogan
item.description: His letter to Danilo Medina records a concrete demand. It also highlights the distinction between a person’s ancestry and legal status.

item.title: Deus Deronneth in 2024: challenging a council is not annulling it
item.description: He invoked sovereignty and separation of powers. Understanding the position requires distinguishing a candidate’s argument from a judicial decision.

item.title: Salomon and OPL: opposing a council that included another party leader
item.description: A 2025 protest in Les Cayes shows why a party does not always speak with one voice. Connections and disagreements both need documenting.

item.title: Joanas Gué and mango exports in 2007: reopening did not end the crisis
item.description: An announced mid-July restart was followed by another suspension at month-end. Following the dates changes the assessment.

item.title: Joanas Gué after the 2008 storms: losses are not recovery funding
item.description: Damage estimates, recovery plans and budget funding are separate stages. Combining them makes a public response harder to assess.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque and Mouka: a public resource behind the speech
item.description: A 2023 address on women’s rights points to a verifiable institutional action. It offers a way to examine the record of a rector seeking office.

item.title: Dominique Dupuy: after condemning deportations, what protection followed?
item.description: A 2024 official communiqué records the diplomatic task assigned to her. Assessing the record requires following what happened to the people affected.

item.title: René St-Fort: displacement should not erase a vote
item.description: His registration position highlights an easily missed barrier: an office can remain open while the citizen cannot reach it.

item.title: Nestor, Savary and DPA: a launch did not settle every affiliation
item.description: Dated records show why appearing at a political event does not, by itself, establish someone’s eventual party affiliation.

item.title: Michelet Nestor: modest origins, big promises and the record
item.description: A 2015 profile records the social story accompanying his political entry. A life story provides context; it does not replace evidence of management.

item.title: Deus Deronneth: waiting for security, but until when?
item.description: His criticism of changing electoral rules raises a real difficulty: protecting voters while keeping the transition time-bound.

item.title: Hans Joseph: leaving ULCC and claiming independence
item.description: The former director offers an explanation for his dismissal. His account and a proven motive are different things.

item.title: René St-Fort and 30,000 supporters: a citizen’s name is not a blank signature
item.description: PRN’s challenge opens a debate about consent. Enabling verification need not expose everyone’s political choices.

item.title: René St-Fort: a common curriculum needs the means to teach it
item.description: His education proposals connect two issues: what children should learn and the conditions of those who teach them.

item.title: Wilson Jeudy in 2016: four million in cash, more than 18 million in payroll
item.description: A simple comparison explains the problem he described. It does not establish responsibility or trace every gourde.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu and governors: autonomy still needs accountability
item.description: The 2025 dispute reaches beyond the word “federal.” It concerns who manages departmental money and who can demand accounts.

item.title: Claude Joseph in July 2021: emergency power and a handover
item.description: After Jovenel Moïse’s assassination, executive authority became an immediate question. Following the sequence allows scrutiny of Joseph’s political record without conflating it with the criminal case.

item.title: Tardieu and Bodeau in 2019: the records, the vote and what it did not settle
item.description: A debate over impeaching Jovenel Moïse ended in a disputed vote. Its political outcome did not adjudicate every financial allegation.

item.title: Jude Célestin: from boycott to a new election
item.description: Challenging an election, obtaining a rerun and winning it are different outcomes. The 2015–2016 crisis illustrates the distinction.

item.title: Jocelerme Privert: what happened after the 120 days
item.description: In 2016, a short timetable became a dispute over continued authority. Contemporary reports help separate the responsibilities.

item.title: Etzer Émile and the Court of Auditors: what limits should a president accept?
item.description: His 2020 criticism opens a question about power: should scrutiny that restrains an opponent remain when you take office?

item.title: Etzer Émile: a late budget and promises needing evidence
item.description: In 2020, the economist questioned the credibility of the government’s timetable and revenue forecasts. The same test can examine his own promises.

item.title: Munir Joseph Mourra: who cares for the patient after the mobile clinic leaves?
item.description: MPH proposes modern hospitals, NGO coordination and mobile clinics. The challenge is making those tools work as a continuing service.

item.title: Joanas Gué: what a 2007 ant campaign reveals about agricultural response
item.description: The problem had been assessed; resources and action were still being arranged. The gap between those stages is where management can be examined.

item.title: Walsonn Sanon: rejecting a pact, then building consent
item.description: Between 2022 and 2025, he challenged political selection and party practices. Those standards also offer a way to examine his own organization.

item.title: Clarens Renois: the signature tying him to transition promises
item.description: He was not a Presidential Council member. His signature on the 2024 agreement nevertheless gives voters a concrete commitment to examine.

item.title: Muscadin: an incomplete file does not settle a candidacy
item.description: A missing-document report, a resignation letter and a registry entry describe three stages. They should not be treated as the same decision.

item.title: Olivier Barrau and farmers’ insurance: when rainfall determines payment
item.description: An AIC–WFP project offers a concrete way to examine the candidate’s experience: whom does insurance protect, and under what conditions?

item.title: Olivier Barrau: AIC’s business grew while profit fell
item.description: Two figures in one report tell different stories. Reading the table carefully changes how the candidate’s business record should be assessed.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu and Royal Oasis: following three different kinds of money
item.description: A loan, a foundation’s share purchase and a later share sale are different transactions. The hotel’s history shows why those distinctions matter.

item.title: Martelly’s son and the 2016 order: a file not ready for judgment
item.description: A headline about a clearance request does not tell the whole decision. The Olivier Martelly record shows what the court decided and what it left open.

item.title: Martelly and the Bautista contracts: the story began before his term
item.description: Contract dates and later decisions matter. They allow responsibility to be traced without assigning every transaction to the same president.

item.title: Hans Joseph: 166 referrals, but who followed them after investigation?
item.description: An ECC inquiry shows why report counts alone cannot measure results against corruption.

item.title: Jude Célestin and CNE: the machines need an inventory, not only a budget
item.description: A Senate report separates the allocation, the contract record and the equipment investigators could verify.

item.title: Martelly and Charles Saint-Rémy: three links to keep distinct
item.description: Family, an advisory role and sanctions are three different facts. Putting them in order makes questions about power more precise.

item.title: Moïse Durocher: one and a half million jobs need more than a large number
item.description: The goal could change many families’ lives. Assessing it requires knowing which jobs, over what period and with what funding.

item.title: Gandhy Dorfeuille: after the electricity launch, what followed?
item.description: An older project with a reported 24-million-gourde budget offers a concrete way to examine the former deputy’s experience.

item.title: Savannah Savary: a civic-work record predating the campaign
item.description: A UN archive documents writing workshops in 2018. Their themes—rights, justice and security—return in this election.

item.title: Savannah Savary: inherited businesses and the power she seeks
item.description: Sugarcane, kleren and land form part of her story. Her account of the family businesses opens a question about private interests and public decisions.

item.title: Wilson Jeudy: what the 2011 camp clearances require us to examine
item.description: Security was the rationale for an operation. Families losing shelter had rights too. The contemporary record puts those responsibilities side by side.

item.title: Muscadin and the 2023 reprimand: security and limits on power
item.description: An earlier ministry letter raises a question that goes beyond a prosecutor’s popularity.

item.title: Muscadin: who owns the armored vehicle donors bought?
item.description: After public fundraising and his resignation, an ownership and accountability question remains.

item.title: Kely Bastien in 2010: what limits should unelected power face?
item.description: After the earthquake, he discussed deadlines and legitimacy. That position belongs in the political record.

item.title: Renois and Maxo Joseph: what the 2015 Protestant candidate selection meant
item.description: An agreement among leaders selected a candidate; it did not transfer citizens’ votes.

item.title: Salomon in 2020: a permanent Senate, but who chose its president?
item.description: An old crisis shows the difference between defending an institution and receiving authority to lead it.

item.title: Wilner Joseph and the VIKTWA primary: two reports, two vote counts
item.description: Both reports name him the winner, but their figures differ. The minutes matter.

item.title: Hans Joseph: reporting corruption should not require a trip to Port-au-Prince
item.description: Two State documents put citizens’ access at the center of the anti-corruption record.

item.title: Hans Joseph: a million dollars on paper, but the houses had not started
item.description: An ULCC document in the OAS archive shows what an image can reveal and what it cannot decide.

item.title: Célestin and Martelly in 2010: 234 tally sheets and a changed runoff
item.description: The OAS report and criticism of its method show why recalculation differs from a full recount.

item.title: Martelly and Bodeau: why foreign sanctions do not automatically settle election eligibility
item.description: Understanding their presence on the registration dashboard requires separating three different decisions.

item.title: Jude Elie: business interests need a clear map
item.description: Two public pages identify starting points for examining private interests, not a complete asset declaration.

item.title: Jude Elie at NYCHA: what an official chart confirms
item.description: A 2018 document provides a specific basis for examining his housing experience.

item.title: Marc Arthur Drouillard and MORED: what the $100 fee offers
item.description: A membership page combines services and political participation. The accounts need to show what each payment funds.

item.title: Munir Mourra proposes an agricultural bank. The credit problem has a history.
item.description: A new institution should explain what changes in a farmer’s life.

item.title: Munir Mourra’s security budgets: what does “100% more” mean?
item.description: Doubling an amount does not automatically double service. The starting point and prices matter.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu and the Constitution: whom did the 2017 consultations reach?
item.description: A communiqué records meetings, but cannot replace submissions and decisions.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu and the diaspora: voting, representation and office differ
item.description: An earlier proposal helps separate questions about participation from abroad.

item.title: Jerry Tardieu: from a PNH bill to a national-guard proposal
item.description: The legislative record and new security proposal need to be read stage by stage.

item.title: Joanas Gué and 115 irrigation systems: repairs need a follow-through
item.description: An old statement on agricultural works opens a record of maintenance and outcomes.

item.title: Joanas Gué called for local buying in 2010. School meals offer a test today.
item.description: An idea can recur across campaigns. The purchasing system determines delivery.

item.title: Déus Deronneth in Marigot: why the first result was not the last word
item.description: An old parliamentary contest shows what a challenge can change, and what it cannot establish.

item.title: Dominique Dupuy: the 2024 threats and two women on the presidential list
item.description: A registration list shows who reaches the door, not every barrier encountered.

item.title: Dominique Dupuy’s diplomatic recalls: what savings followed?
item.description: Making an administration smaller and making it work better are separate outcomes.

item.title: Lucmanne Delille and G9: two dates his account must address
item.description: A UN report and a published account of his 2022 response place G9’s formation differently.

item.title: Kely Bastien: the transparency test predates this campaign
item.description: An old official briefing points to the public record behind the new candidacy.

item.title: Kely Bastien: who selected him for DELIVRANS?
item.description: A coalition’s selection explains its internal organization, not the country’s voting intentions.

item.title: Marc Arthur Drouillard: what a 2016 footnote adds to the small vote total
item.description: An old result does not explain an alliance. The observers’ report adds another piece.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque in 2015: do not merge two clearance files
item.description: A candidate’s name on a decision does not mean it covers every previous role.

item.title: Jacky Lumarque: the vocational-training test starts before the campaign
item.description: An education career supplies experience to examine, not results to assume.

item.title: Olivier Barrau’s youth corps: who selects and who pays?
item.description: A foundation event differs from a national service that must serve all citizens.

item.title: Olivier Barrau and AIC: the IDB’s $2 million was not a campaign gift
item.description: The 2012 loan record identifies a specific financial relationship and purpose to examine.

item.title: Olivier Barrau: from a family insurance business to presidential ambition
item.description: A business history can explain a career. It cannot replace an account of financial interests.

item.title: Etzer Emile’s school budget: 16% and 22% measure different things
item.description: Money authorized on paper does not always equal money delivered to a service.

item.title: Etzer Emile: 5,000 small projects mean 5 billion gourdes
item.description: The arithmetic is simple. Choosing beneficiaries fairly is the harder test.

item.title: Etzer Emile: 500 megawatts does not explain the electricity bill
item.description: To assess the promise, follow power from the plant to the household.

item.title: Etzer Emile’s $30 billion plan: who provides the money?
item.description: A total shows the scale of a promise. Funding sources show who carries the risk.

item.title: Etzer Emile wants to double the police. When will recruits be ready?
item.description: Announcing training and putting a prepared officer on the street are different steps.

item.title: Privert and Canada: what does the sanctions record establish?
item.description: The list confirms an administrative designation. It does not replace evidence about each alleged act.

item.title: Muscadin: public protection and the 76 cases documented by the UN
item.description: Support for a security official and evidence about his methods are different questions.

item.title: Gary Bodeau: when an appointment vote allegedly had a price
item.description: The U.S. Treasury describes payments intended to influence votes in the Chamber of Deputies. Bodeau disputes the allegations.

item.title: What Martelly’s lobbying contract asks Washington to change
item.description: The document targets sanctions policy. It is neither a verdict nor a promise of success.

item.title: Martelly’s lobbying file: who is paying?
item.description: A U.S. filing reports $75,000 received; the contract specifies other amounts. Those are different facts.

item.title: 54 Palace rifles: where a family connection meets public responsibility
item.description: The UN report names a security official and a family connection. The public role and the weapons trail must be examined together.

item.title: Martelly and gangs: what the UN report says about intermediaries
item.description: The 2023 report describes money, weapons and people connecting them. Each link needs its own evidence.

item.title: Martelly: what do the three U.S. restrictions cover?
item.description: The word “sanctions” covers specific measures. Their actual terms matter.

item.title: After Martelly’s school promise, demand clear accounts
item.description: Our editorial position: a promise to serve children should include a way for the public to check each stage of the money trail.

item.title: Claude Joseph and the Moïse case: what changed after 2024
item.description: Understanding the case requires following Haiti’s inquiry and the U.S. prosecutions separately, including what happened after the first accusations.

item.title: School-fee money: the accounting problem continued
item.description: A report covering 2023–2024 says FNE revenue was counted in the government budget balance while its spending was left out. Why does that matter?

item.title: Martelly and Privert: what did the school-fee lawsuit allege?
item.description: A group of U.S. residents challenged the transfer and call charges. Here are their allegations, the court’s response and the limits of the evidence.

item.title: Martelly and the $1.50 fee: what were families paying for?
item.description: Under Martelly, a transfer fee became part of a promise of free schooling. A lawsuit later challenged how the arrangement worked.
